questions.stem: A team's PCI DSS scope lists the switch and its database. A build server, which never stores or receives a card number, deploys every release to the switch. Where does the build server stand?

options.text: In scope, since each release it deploys changes the code that runs where the card numbers are
options.says: the CDE includes every system able to affect the security of a card data system; a build server can ship a build that copies every card number

options.text: In scope, since the switch's card numbers pass through it while each release is deployed
options.says: the stem says no card number reaches it; it is in scope for what it can change on the switch, not for data passing through

options.text: Out of scope, since the card numbers never reach it in any of the releases it deploys
options.says: the misconception the page names: only systems with card numbers count; it leaves the build server without controls

options.text: Out of scope, since each release it deploys is signed and reviewed before the switch runs it
options.says: signing does not change that the build server can change what runs on the switch; scope follows what a system can reach and affect

origin.section: 13.1. PCI DSS Covers Every System That Touches Card Data, and Every System That Can Reach One

questions.stem: A reversal queue runs on a Berkeley DB space. Last night's reversals were cloned from their purchases, and all of them were answered, so the queue is empty this morning. A text search of the store's files for the card numbers finds nothing. What do the files hold?

options.text: Nothing from last night, since an answered reversal is removed from the queue and from the file
options.says: taking an entry out appends a deletion to Berkeley DB's log; the old bytes stay until the cleaner deletes the file

options.text: Nothing from last night, since the search would show any card number the files still hold
options.says: Berkeley DB stores byte arrays with the top bit of each byte flipped, so a plain text search finds nothing although the data is there

options.text: The cloned card numbers only, encrypted by the store, which is why the search missed them
options.says: the store does not encrypt; it keeps whole messages, and a clone carries track 2 and the PIN block as well as the card number

options.text: The cloned reversals in full, encoded by the store, which is why the search missed them
options.says: the cloned reversals carried every field, tracks and PIN blocks included; the log keeps them after they are taken out, encoded so a text search misses them

origin.section: 13.3. Card Data Ends Up Where Nobody Meant to Store It

questions.stem: Ten days before certification, the dependency scanner marks an XML library that jPOS pulls in as critical. The finding is real, but the vulnerable parser only reads the deploy files at start-up, and only administrators can change those files. What do you do?

options.text: Defer it with a risk acceptance naming an owner and a review date, since the path is closed
options.says: an unexposed finding can be deferred, with an owner, a review date and the event that would reopen it written down

options.text: Close it as not applicable with the reachability analysis attached, since the path is closed
options.says: the finding is confirmed; closing it drops the owner, the review date and the event that would reopen it, which a deferral keeps

options.text: Override the library in tonight's build and attach the new scan, since the fix is a small step
options.says: an override is the lighter fix when the issue is real and exposed; a change days before certification carries its own risk

options.text: Upgrade jPOS before certification and rerun the full test plan, since the finding is critical
options.says: severity is the component's worst case; with no exposure, a rushed upgrade in the payment path is the larger risk

origin.section: 13.5. A Scanner Finding Is a Question, and the Answer Is Written Down

questions.stem: Legal decides that a cardholder's transaction records stay for the retention period and everything else about them is erased. The processor stores card numbers only encrypted, in its transaction and dispute tables. What does the system need to carry this out?

options.text: A plain hash stored beside each record, since it finds the person's records without a clear card number
options.says: the page asks for keyed values, not plain hashes, which unit s9 reverses in a quarter of a second

options.text: A keyed lookup value beside each record, since it finds the person's records without a clear card number
options.says: the keyed lookup of unit s9 finds a card's records without storing the number in clear, which erasure and export need

options.text: A search of every store for the card number in clear, since the person's data is wherever it appears
options.says: the tables hold the number only encrypted, so a search for it in clear finds none of the person's records

options.text: A search of every store for the card number masked, since the person's data is wherever it appears
options.says: a masked number keeps only six and four digits, which many cards share, and the encrypted tables don't hold it either

origin.section: 13.7. Data Protection Law Covers the Same Records and Can Ask for the Opposite
